planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this dwarf alpine species tulip from Iran, eastern Turkey, and the Caucasus needs a hot, dry summer dormancy to persist for more than a season or two.

directions: Tulipa humilis is a dwarf alpine species tulip native to rocky slopes and screes of Iran, eastern Turkey, and the Caucasus, opening wide, fragrant, magenta-to-rose-pink flowers with a striking blue-black and yellow basal blotch over low tufts of narrow gray-green leaves in the first weeks of true spring. Because it comes from a region of cold, dry winters and hot, dry summers, it strongly prefers lean, gritty, sharply drained soil and a baking summer dormancy, performing far better in a rock garden, raised trough, or gravel bed than in a typical rich, irrigated border. Several named selections such as 'Persian Pearl' trace back to this wild species, but the species form itself is an inexpensive way to trial the type and is, if anything, closer to its tough mountain origins. Left undisturbed in suitable conditions it slowly multiplies by offsets, forming a long-lived clump rather than declining after a season or two like many modern hybrid tulips.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; native to Central Asian steppe and foothill terrain, it requires a dry summer rest and resents soggy winter soil.

directions: Tulipa batalinii is a diminutive species tulip from the rocky steppe and foothill terrain of Central Asia, bearing a single slender, pale creamy-yellow goblet flower per stem above a low rosette of narrow, often faintly wavy, blue-green leaves. It is the wild parent behind several well-known soft-colored dwarf tulip selections sold in the bulb trade, but the species itself remains available and offers the same refined, understated coloring in an unimproved form. Give it the baking-hot, bone-dry summer rest and sharp winter drainage it would experience in its native habitat, since wet soil during dormancy is the most common cause of failure with this and other Central Asian species tulips. Its small scale and subtle color make it well suited to a trough, scree bed, or the front edge of a sunny rock garden rather than a conventional mixed border.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species typically carries several small star-shaped flowers per bulb and needs a hot, dry summer dormancy.

directions: Tulipa urumiensis is named for the saline Lake Urmia basin of northwestern Iran, where it grows on dry, rocky, gravelly slopes, and it is unusual among dwarf species tulips in typically carrying two to four small star-shaped flowers on branching stems from a single bulb rather than just one. The petals open bright golden-yellow with a bronze-to-maroon flush on their outer surfaces, so the tightly closed buds show more bronze than gold until they open fully in sunshine. Like its Middle Eastern relatives it needs a hot, completely dry summer dormancy and sharply drained, lean soil to persist beyond a season or two. It suits raised gritty beds, rock gardens, and container culture, where its multi-flowered habit gives a fuller display per bulb than many single-flowered species tulips.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; among the earliest tulips to bloom, it usually carries two or more small star-shaped flowers per stem.

directions: Tulipa biflora is one of the earliest tulips to bloom, often opening small, fragrant, star-shaped flowers not long after the first crocus, with creamy white petals flushed gray-green or bronze on the reverse and a bright yellow central blotch. True to its name it typically produces two or more flowers per stem from a single bulb, a trait shared with the closely related and sometimes-confused Tulipa turkestanica, though biflora tends to be slightly smaller in stature overall. Native to rocky and steppe habitats from the Caucasus through Central Asia, it demands sharp drainage and a dry summer rest, thriving in gritty rock-garden or trough conditions rather than a conventional moist border. Plant it toward the front of a sunny, well-drained bed where its modest height won't be lost among later, taller spring bulbs.

common_name: Crocus Flavus (Wild Ancestor of the Dutch Yellow Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this Balkan and Turkish wild species is the principal ancestor of the giant Dutch yellow crocus hybrids sold for mass display.

directions: Crocus flavus is a wild species from the Balkan Peninsula and northwestern Turkey and is the principal ancestor of the giant golden Dutch crocus hybrids sold for mass garden display, though the true species itself is smaller and, many growers feel, more refined and fragrant than its hybrid descendants. Each corm sends up slender, deep golden-orange, goblet-shaped flowers with a faint honeyed scent in late winter to earliest spring, often appearing while the ground is still bare or lightly frosted. It is an easy, reliable grower in full sun and well-drained soil, naturalizing readily by offsets and self-seeding in lawns, rock gardens, and border edges. Allow the grass-like foliage to yellow and die back completely before mowing if naturalized in turf, so the corms can store energy for next year's bloom.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; native to dry rocky hillsides near Ankara, Turkey, it bears an unusually generous cluster of orange-yellow flowers per corm.

directions: Crocus ancyrensis takes its name from Ankara, the Turkish capital near which it grows wild on dry, rocky, scrubby hillsides, and it is notable for producing an unusually generous cluster of four to six small, bright orange-yellow flowers from a single corm, all opening together for a dense, bunched display rather than the single or paired blooms typical of most crocus species. The widely grown selection 'Golden Bunch' was selected directly from this wild species and shares its vigorous clump-forming habit and very early bloom time, often among the first crocuses to open in late winter. Give the species form full sun and sharp drainage, since like most Turkish crocus species it dislikes being wet during its summer dormancy. It multiplies readily by cormlets, forming dense clumps within a few seasons in a rock garden, gravel bed, or front border position.

common_name: Cloth of Gold Crocus (Narrow-Leaved Wild Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this historic Crimean species has been grown in European gardens since at least the sixteenth century as the 'Cloth of Gold' crocus.

directions: Crocus angustifolius, long grown in European gardens as the historic 'Cloth of Gold' crocus, has been cultivated since at least the sixteenth century for its brilliant deep yellow-orange flowers, the outer three petals boldly feathered and striped with bronze-purple on their outer face so that closed buds show far more purple-brown than gold until the flowers open flat in the sun. Native to rocky grassland and scrub of Crimea and the surrounding Black Sea region, it is a tough, easy, long-persisting species that multiplies steadily into dense clumps when grown in full sun with sharp winter drainage. Its narrow, grass-like leaves, each marked with a fine white midrib stripe, help distinguish it from other small early crocus species even before it flowers. Being one of the oldest garden crocuses in continuous cultivation, it predates nearly all of the modern Dutch hybrid crocus cultivars grown today.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this Balkan alpine species flowers as mountain snow retreats and resents summer wet.

directions: Crocus veluchensis takes its name from Mount Velouchi in central Greece and grows naturally in subalpine and alpine meadows across the mountains of Greece, Albania, and neighboring Balkan countries, flowering as winter snow retreats at elevation, which in garden cultivation translates to an early-to-mid spring bloom. Its lilac-to-violet-purple flowers often show darker feathering toward the base and a paler, sometimes near-white throat, with the silvery-grey exterior of the unopened buds giving way to much brighter color once open in sun. As a true alpine species it appreciates gritty, humus-light, very sharply drained soil and resents summer wet more than many other spring crocuses, making it better suited to a scree bed or trough than a conventional border. It is less commonly offered than Crocus tommasinianus or C. chrysanthus but is worthwhile for rock-garden and alpine enthusiasts wanting to diversify their early-season crocus collection.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; native to the eastern Mediterranean, it prefers a drier summer rest than woodland snowdrop species.

directions: Galanthus fosteri is native to rocky woodland and scrub from Lebanon and Syria through southern Turkey, named for the nineteenth-century plantsman Michael Foster who helped popularize several Eastern Mediterranean snowdrop species in Western gardens. It is distinguished by broad, often glossy dark green leaves and comparatively large flowers whose inner segments usually carry green markings at both the tip and the base, giving a bolder two-toned green pattern than the simple notch seen on common snowdrop. Coming from a region with hot, dry summers, it benefits from a drier summer dormancy than woodland species such as G. nivalis and performs best where soil isn't kept constantly moist once the foliage dies down. Plant bulbs, or divide and move clumps 'in the green' just after flowering, into humus-rich soil in dappled shade for a reliable, very early show of late-winter flowers.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this Caucasus mountain species wants reliable winter cold and sharp drainage rather than constant moisture.

directions: Galanthus alpinus grows wild in subalpine and alpine meadows of the Caucasus Mountains, where it pushes up through retreating snow at considerable elevation, a habit that has earned the broader alpinus group a reputation among galanthophiles as tricky to satisfy in lowland gardens used to milder, wetter winters. Its broad, often blue-green leaves and relatively robust, rounded white flowers distinguish it from the more commonly grown G. nivalis, though the species is less often available and best suited to collectors with a cool, well-drained, humus-rich site that mimics its mountain origin. Give it a position with reliable winter cold, sharp drainage, and some summer dryness rather than the constantly moist woodland conditions suited to many other snowdrop species. As with other uncommon Galanthus species, sourcing from a reputable specialist bulb nursery is advisable, since true alpinus is less widely propagated than many garden-standard snowdrops.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; named for its unusually wide, glossy leaves, among the broadest of any snowdrop species.

directions: Galanthus platyphyllus is named for its exceptionally broad, glossy, strap-like leaves, among the widest of any snowdrop species, which emerge folded together and spread considerably by the time flowering finishes. Native to the Caucasus region, its rounded white flowers are typically unmarked or only very faintly marked with green on the outer segments, giving a purer white effect than many other snowdrops whose look is often set off by boldly marked inner segments. Like other Caucasian snowdrop species it appreciates humus-rich but well-drained woodland soil and benefits from division and replanting while still 'in the green,' shortly after flowering finishes in late winter. Its broad foliage makes it a particularly handsome choice for a shaded collector's bed where the leaves can be appreciated as much as the flowers.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; native to the wetter Black Sea coast of northeastern Turkey.

directions: Galanthus rizehensis takes its name from Rize province on Turkey's eastern Black Sea coast, a notably wet and humid region for a snowdrop species, which may explain why this species tolerates damper growing conditions better than many of its drier-summer Mediterranean relatives. Its narrow, somewhat glaucous leaves and relatively small, rounded flowers with a single green mark on each inner segment place it among the less showy Caucasian-Turkish snowdrop species, but it is valued by collectors for extending the snowdrop season and for its distinct regional origin. Plant bulbs in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but still well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it can receive steadier moisture through the growing season than its drier-summer relatives prefer. Division and replanting 'in the green' shortly after flowering is the most reliable way to establish new clumps of this still relatively uncommon species.

subcategory: Western US native dry spring bulb

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in sharply drained, mineral soil in full sun to light shade; this hummingbird-pollinated native of northern California and southern Oregon requires a strict dry summer dormancy.

directions: Scarlet fritillary is a hummingbird-pollinated species native to dry montane forest and chaparral margins of northern California and southern Oregon, sending up slender stems hung with several narrow, bell-shaped flowers whose vivid orange-scarlet exterior is checkered inside with yellow, a color combination unusual among fritillaries and clearly aimed at bird rather than insect pollinators. It is considered one of the more challenging fritillary species to establish in cultivation, requiring the same sharply drained, mineral soil and strict dry summer dormancy it experiences on its native dry slopes, where winter and spring moisture is followed by a long rainless summer. Grow it in a raised bed, bulb frame, or gritty native-plant rock garden rather than an irrigated border, and avoid any summer watering once the foliage has yellowed. Because bulbs can be slow to establish and wild populations are easily disturbed, source only nursery-propagated bulbs from a reputable native-plant or specialty bulb supplier.

subcategory: Western US native dry spring bulb

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; this California coastal grassland native goes fully dormant for a long dry summer and should never be watered once foliage yellows.

directions: Fritillaria biflora, commonly called mission bells, is a California native found on coastal bluffs, grassy slopes, and occasionally serpentine soils from the Bay Area south into Baja California, and like its close relative Fritillaria affinis (grown as 'chocolate lily') it bears nodding, bell-shaped flowers in deep chocolate-brown to blackish-purple, often mottled with dull greenish-yellow, though mission bells typically carries fewer flowers per stem and favors drier, more open coastal grassland than the woodland-edge sites F. affinis prefers. Flowering from February into April depending on location, it goes dormant for the long dry California summer and should never be watered once the foliage yellows. Plant bulbs in fall in fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the open coastal grassland and bluff conditions of its native range. As with many California native bulbs, it is best purchased as nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected material.

subcategory: Western US native dry spring bulb

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in sharply drained, often clay or serpentine-derived soil in full sun; this rare San Francisco Bay Area native requires dry summer dormancy and should be sourced only as nursery-propagated stock.

directions: Fritillaria liliacea is a rare California endemic, now largely restricted to scattered grassland and serpentine-soil remnants around the San Francisco Bay Area and the central coast after extensive habitat loss to development and agriculture, which has made conservation-minded gardeners and native plant societies especially interested in its cultivation. Unlike most fritillaries, its nodding, bell-shaped flowers are a plain creamy white rather than checkered, and they carry a distinct, pleasant fragrance unusual within the genus. It requires the same dry summer dormancy and sharply drained, often clay or serpentine-derived soil typical of its native grassland habitat, and resents summer irrigation. Because of its rarity in the wild, gardeners should source only nursery-propagated bulbs from reputable California native plant nurseries, never wild-collected material, when adding this species to a native bulb collection.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this later-blooming, drought-tolerant species tolerates heat better than many garden grape hyacinths.

directions: Muscari tenuiflorum is a slender, loosely flowered grape hyacinth from the dry grasslands and steppe of southeastern Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Caucasus, related to the showier tassel hyacinth (M. comosum) but notably more delicate, with an open, airy raceme rather than a tight, congested spike. The lower, fertile flowers are a muted grey-brown to dusky blue-violet with a paler rim, topped by a small tuft of brighter blue-violet sterile flowers that gives the spike a subtle two-toned effect on close inspection, though the overall look is far less flamboyant than M. comosum 'Plumosum'. Flowering later than most grape hyacinths, typically in May, it tolerates heat and drier summer conditions better than many garden muscari, reflecting its steppe origins. Grow it in full sun in average, well-drained soil, where it naturalizes modestly among other dry-growing bulbs and perennials.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in light shade; this vigorous Turkish and Balkan species carries far more flowers per raceme than Scilla siberica.

directions: Scilla bithynica takes its name from Bithynia, the ancient region of northwestern Turkey where it grows wild alongside populations in the adjacent Balkans, and it is easily told apart from the more commonly planted Scilla siberica by its looser, more crowded raceme carrying up to a dozen or more small, star-shaped violet-blue flowers per stem rather than just a few. It blooms slightly later in spring than Siberian squill, extending the blue-squill season in a naturalized planting, and spreads readily by both offsets and self-sown seedlings once established in congenial conditions. Plant bulbs in fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in light shade beneath deciduous trees and shrubs, where it can take advantage of the open canopy to bloom and set seed before leaf-out shades the ground. Its vigorous, easy-going nature makes it an excellent choice for naturalizing in woodland-edge plantings alongside snowdrops and early crocus.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, humus-light soil in full sun; this Caucasian alpine species wants sharp drainage and resents disturbance once established.

directions: Scilla rosenii is a Caucasian alpine species whose sharply reflexed, backward-curving tepals and prominently protruding stamens give each small blue-violet flower a distinctive 'shooting star' silhouette quite unlike the more familiar open, bell- or star-shaped flowers of Scilla siberica or S. bifolia. Flowering very early, often alongside the first snowdrops and crocus, it is a true alpine plant best suited to a scree bed, trough, or alpine house rather than a general border, since it wants sharp drainage and resents being disturbed once established. It is slower to multiply and generally considered more challenging in cultivation than the common garden squills, making it more of a specialist collector's plant than a mass-naturalizing bulb. Source bulbs from a specialist alpine or bulb nursery, and plant in a gritty, humus-light mix in full sun with excellent winter drainage.

subcategory: miniature winter-blooming North African hoop-petticoat daffodil species

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained compost in full sun; this North African species is more tender than N. bulbocodium and is usually grown in an alpine house or cold frame.

directions: Narcissus romieuxii is a winter-blooming hoop-petticoat daffodil from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, opening its broad, funnel-shaped, pale lemon-yellow to near-white corona as early as December or January in mild climates, well ahead of the related but hardier Narcissus bulbocodium. Because it comes from a milder North African climate, it is more tender than the true hoop petticoat daffodil and is usually grown as an alpine house or cold frame subject in colder regions, though it can be tried outdoors in sheltered, very well-drained sites in the mildest zones. Its delicate, almost translucent flowers and strong, sweet fragrance have made it a favorite for winter pot culture among specialist bulb growers, often brought into bloom around the winter holidays. Give it gritty, sharply drained compost, a sunny position, and a dry summer rest to replicate the hot, dry Moroccan summer it experiences in the wild.

subcategory: miniature High Atlas alpine daffodil species

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, humus-light compost in full sun; this High Atlas alpine species is hardier than most North African daffodils but is best displayed in a scree bed or trough.

directions: Narcissus watieri is a diminutive wild daffodil from the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco, growing at considerable elevation on rocky slopes where it experiences colder winters than most other North African daffodil species, making it somewhat hardier in cultivation than its lowland relatives. Its pure white flowers, carried singly on very short stems above grass-like foliage, show a small, shallow, saucer-shaped corona rather than the flared hoop-petticoat shape of related species, giving it an elegant, understated look prized by alpine and trough gardeners. It is slow-growing and best displayed in a raised scree bed, trough, or alpine house where its small scale won't be lost among larger plants and where drainage can be kept sharp through its summer dormancy. Plant bulbs shallowly in gritty, humus-light compost in full sun, and avoid any summer moisture once the foliage has died down.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; this ancient double daffodil increases slowly and resents frequent division.

directions: Narcissus 'Eystettensis', widely known as Queen Anne's Double Daffodil, is among the oldest named daffodil cultivars still in cultivation, illustrated in Basilius Besler's 1613 florilegium Hortus Eystettensis, from which it takes its modern cultivar name. Its pale lemon-yellow flowers are fully double, built from neat, symmetrical whorls of narrow, slightly twisted segments that give the bloom a distinctive pompon-like appearance quite unlike later double daffodil hybrids. Thought to be a very old sporting form derived from wild Narcissus pseudonarcissus, it increases slowly and is often grown and passed along by heirloom bulb enthusiasts and historic garden restorations rather than mass-marketed commercially. Plant bulbs in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun, and allow clumps to remain undisturbed for several years, since this heirloom cultivar resents frequent division and takes time to settle in and bloom well.
sources: Old House Gardens Heirloom Bulbs — historic daffodil offerings
